strengths: Provides an exact geometric characterization of feasible (PPV, FOR) pairs for finite-valued calibrated scores, proving star-convexity and deriving the boundary via soft thresholding/fractional knapsack (Theorems 3.3 and 3.4).

Extends the analysis to multiple groups under sufficiency by characterizing the intersection of group-feasible regions as the pointwise maximum of group boundaries, with a boundary-tracing algorithm (Algorithm 1) that handles piecewise hyperbolic arcs and crossing points.

Shows that both loss-minimizing and deviation-from-separation-minimizing sufficient classifiers lie on the boundary of the intersection, and reduces the search to solving quadratic equations, making the approach practical for finite score support.
Addresses a gap left by Baumann et al. (2022) by avoiding continuity and full-support assumptions; it handles arbitrary finite supports and even disjoint supports across groups.
Includes a COMPAS case study showing that the fair optimum achieves accuracy close to the unconstrained optimum and illustrates the necessity of group-specific thresholds.
weaknesses: The central assumption that scores are exactly group-calibrated is strong. Many real-world scores, including COMPAS, are only approximately calibrated. The paper provides no finite-sample calibration or estimation-error analysis, and the algorithm assumes exact knowledge of the score distributions and calibration curve.

Empirical validation is limited to a single dataset with no comparison to existing fair post-processing baselines (e.g., equalized-odds post-processing or Baumann et al.) and no uncertainty quantification, making the practical claims less convincing.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or supplementary material is provided, and the COMPAS experiment lacks details such as random seeds, exact per-group calibration estimation, and how non-monotone calibrated scores are handled.

Presentation issues: the meaning of 'S>=7' in the COMPAS example is ambiguous given non-monotone calibrated scores; notation reuses pi for aggregate and group base rates; the WLOG claim that l00=l11=0 can be achieved by flipping labels is inaccurate (though constant subtraction works).

There is no dedicated limitations or broader-impact section, and degenerate classifiers (constant within a group) are treated separately in Appendix D but are not integrated into the main algorithm or optimization pipeline.

The claim of a 'wide class of objectives' is not formalized; only loss functions depending on p, q, mu and the specific deviation-from-separation measure are optimized, so the title's 'optimal classification' is somewhat broader than what is actually delivered.

strengths: Provides an exact geometric characterization of the feasible region of PPV/FOR pairs for finite, group-calibrated scores, using a fractional knapsack argument and star-convexity.

Derives a simple post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) that traces the boundary of the intersection of group-wise feasible regions under sufficiency, with an efficient interval-based search and quadratic root finding.

Extends the framework to loss minimization and minimization of deviation from separation, showing both objectives can be optimized on the same boundary and reduced to solving quadratics on each interval.
The theoretical results are clearly stated and the appendices provide detailed proofs and algorithmic derivations.
The COMPAS example illustrates the practical possibility of group-specific thresholds achieving near-unconstrained accuracy while satisfying sufficiency.
weaknesses: The method assumes exact group-calibration, P(Y=1|S=s,A=a)=s, for all groups. This is a very strong assumption rarely met in practice; the paper provides no analysis of finite-sample calibration error or robustness. The COMPAS example calibrates globally rather than group-wise and does not verify group-calibration on held-out data, undermining the practical demonstration.

Degenerate classifiers that are constant within a group (e.g., R=A) can satisfy sufficiency and may be optimal, but the main algorithm assumes nonconstant classifiers within each group (0<μ^a<1). Appendix D discusses degenerate cases but does not integrate them into Algorithm 1, so the claimed exact solution may miss optimal sufficient classifiers in some settings.

Empirical validation is weak: only one dataset is used, there is no separate test set for evaluating the resulting classifier, no error bars, and no comparison to relevant baselines such as Baumann et al. (2022), Canetti et al. (2019), or simple thresholding/randomized thresholding. The example reports accuracy but no fairness metrics (group-wise PPV/FOR, sufficiency violation).

Reproducibility is limited: no code, no details on the calibration procedure (e.g., isotonic regression, binning), random splits, or hyperparameters. The COMPAS description is internally inconsistent: it states calibrated scores are not monotone in the original bin ordering, yet interprets optimal rules as original thresholds S≥7/S≥6, and Figure 3 labels dots as R=1 iff S≥1, etc.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section and any discussion of ethical/legal implications of using race-aware post-processing in high-stakes domains such as criminal justice and admissions. No broader impact statement is provided.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work on sufficiency and post-processing. The finite discrete extension is a straightforward application of fractional knapsack, and the paper does not theoretically compare or relate its solution to existing continuous-score methods.

Presentation issues: dense notation, some figures are not self-contained, there is no conclusion, and the scope of the optimality claim (optimal only among classifiers based on S, conditional on exact calibration) is not clearly discussed.

strengths: The paper gives an exact characterization of the feasible PPV/FOR region for finite, group-calibrated scores, extending sufficiency-based post-processing to discrete scores where prior work (e.g., Baumann et al., 2022) relied on continuity/full support.

The geometric development is rigorous: it establishes star-convexity of the feasible region, solves the fixed-selection-rate problem via fractional knapsack, and derives explicit piecewise hyperbolic boundary formulas.

Algorithm 1 provides a clean boundary-tracing procedure for the intersection of group-wise feasible regions, including active-boundary crossings via quadratic conditions, and applies directly to loss minimization and separation-deviation minimization.

The COMPAS case study illustrates the practical relevance of the framework, showing that the fair optimum can require group-specific thresholds and can achieve accuracy close to the unconstrained optimum.
The paper is generally well organized, with detailed derivations and proofs in the appendices, making the main theoretical claims easy to follow.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is limited to a single real dataset, with no synthetic experiments or comparisons to existing sufficiency post-processing methods, so the practical superiority/robustness of the approach is not convincingly established.

The method relies on exact group-calibration of the scores; in the COMPAS example the calibration curve is estimated from a 20% split and sufficiency is only approximately assumed, but no error analysis or robustness discussion is provided.

The loss-minimization analysis assumes without loss of generality that ℓ00 = ℓ11 = 0; for general loss matrices this normalization is not fully justified, and if the relevant coefficient is positive the optimum may involve degenerate/constant classifiers rather than the nontrivial boundary.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is released, and the empirical calibration procedure, random splits, and exact estimation steps are not specified in enough detail to reproduce the reported accuracy numbers.
The paper does not include a limitations section and does not discuss the ethical implications of applying race-aware post-processing to high-stakes criminal-justice data such as COMPAS.

Some key structural claims, e.g., that the boundary of the intersection determines the entire feasible intersection, rely on an upper-set/vertical-convexity property that is used implicitly but not fully proved in the main text.

strengths: Provides an exact geometric characterization of the feasible (PPV, FOR) pairs attainable by classifiers based on finite group-calibrated scores, with a complete boundary description and proof (Theorem 3.4), filling a gap between continuous full-support assumptions in prior work and practical finite-score settings.

Derives an efficient boundary-tracing algorithm (Algorithm 1) for the intersection of group-wise feasible regions, enabling exact optimization under sufficiency for loss minimization and deviation from separation.

Shows that loss-optimal and separation-deviation-minimizing sufficient classifiers lie on the boundary of the feasible intersection, reducing optimization to evaluating interval endpoints and critical points of rational functions; extends to arbitrary losses with zero diagonal costs.

Provides a robustness analysis for calibration error, proving PPV/FOR violations are bounded by twice the maximum calibration error, with synthetic and ACS experiments showing practical violations well below the bound.

Includes an end-to-end ACS Income experiment over 100 train/test splits, showing the post-processed classifier reduces PPV and FOR gaps by roughly an order of magnitude with only a small accuracy drop relative to the unconstrained baseline.
Clear presentation with detailed appendices, an honest discussion of limitations (e.g., multi-group feasibility, approximate calibration), and a thoughtful impact statement.
weaknesses: The central assumption of exact group-calibration of finite scores is strong; in practice scores are only approximately calibrated, so the exact fairness guarantee may not hold, as even the ACS experiment shows small nonzero PPV/FOR gaps.

No empirical comparison to prior sufficiency-based methods (e.g., Canetti et al. abstention, Baumann et al. utility maximization under sufficiency, Zeng et al. fair Bayes-optimal under predictive parity). Experiments only compare to an unconstrained Bayes classifier, so the practical advantage over existing fair post-processing approaches remains unclear.

The COMPAS experiment constructs group-calibrated scores by pooling empirical outcome rates ignoring group membership and then treats them as group-calibrated; this is somewhat circular and does not test robustness to real miscalibration. Only the ACS experiment is a realistic end-to-end test.
No code availability or reproducibility statement is provided; while the algorithm and experimental details are described, an implementation would aid reproducibility and adoption.

Exact sufficiency for multiple groups can be infeasible, and the paper acknowledges this but does not provide an approximate method for when the intersection of group-wise feasible regions is empty, limiting practical applicability in such cases.
The boundary-tracing algorithm iterates over O(m^0 m^1) intervals, which may become costly for large score supports; computational complexity and scalability are not discussed.
Loss minimization is restricted to losses with ℓ00 = ℓ11 = 0, which does not cover all possible loss functions of interest.

strengths: Provides a clean, complete and correct geometric characterization of the feasible (PPV, FOR) region for finite-valued calibrated scores, including the explicit piecewise boundary (hyperbolic arcs plus a vertical segment) and its breakpoints at deterministic thresholds.

The theoretical arguments are sound: the fractional-knapsack/greedy selection rule (Theorem 3.3), the star-convexity argument, the fixed-μ monotonicity of the loss and of Δ_sep, and the pointwise-max description of the intersection boundary (Eq. 10) are all correct, and the reduction of optimal fair classification to optimization over ∂(C^0∩C^1) follows.
The resulting post-processing algorithm is simple and efficient, and requires only group-calibrated scores and group membership, with no retraining or raw features.

The ACS Income experiment is a genuine end-to-end evaluation (100 train/test splits, out-of-fold calibration, bootstrap confidence intervals) showing small PPV/FOR gaps with modest accuracy loss, and the robustness analysis (Appendix J) gives a useful linear 2ε bound on parity violation under calibration error.
Writing is clear and the figures are informative.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core machinery is standard (greedy LP/fractional knapsack, star-convex feasible regions, intersection of two regions via pointwise max). The single-group characterization is close to prior work (Canetti et al. 2019; Baumann et al. 2022), and the main advance is removing the continuity/full-support assumptions of Baumann et al., which is a relatively incremental step.

The optimal classifier is randomized (soft thresholding on the boundary bin), yet the paper never discusses the serious practical, legal and ethical problems of randomized decisions in precisely the high-stakes domains that motivate it (bail/COMPAS, lending, admissions). This omission is material given the framing and the Impact Statement.

The COMPAS experiment is arguably not a valid test of the method: scores are declared 'group-calibrated' by assigning pooled (group-agnostic) empirical rates to deciles, so P(Y=1|S=d,A=a)≠s_d in general. The empirical claims there do not actually exercise the calibration assumption the theory relies on.

Empirical comparison is weak: the only baseline is the unconstrained Bayes classifier. There is no comparison against prior sufficiency methods (e.g., Canetti et al.'s abstention-based classifiers or Baumann et al.'s post-processing), which would be the natural points of reference and would clarify whether randomization/intersection offers practical gains.

The 'minimizing deviation from separation' section is somewhat ad hoc (it adopts the Δ_sep measure of Benger & Ligett 2025), and its central practical claim—that the resulting classifier 'often achieves performance comparable to the optimum'—is supported only by a few examples, not theoretically.

The central assumption of exact group-calibration is strong, and in the only end-to-end experiment it is only approximately satisfied, so the exactness guarantees of the method are not realized in practice (guarantees hold only up to 2ε).

The multi-group setting, which the paper itself identifies as the practically important case, is only partially addressed: feasibility of the intersection becomes more restrictive with more groups, and this limitation is relegated to future work.

strengths: Provides a clean and rigorous geometric characterization of the feasible (PPV, FOR) region for finite, group-calibrated scores. The star-convexity argument, the fractional-knapsack/greedy thresholding result (Theorem 3.3), and the piecewise hyperbolic boundary with breakpoints at deterministic thresholds (Theorem 3.4) are correct and elegantly presented.

Delivers an exact solution to optimal (randomized) classification under sufficiency: it correctly shows that for fixed selection rate the loss (Eq. 12/13) and the deviation-from-separation (Eq. 14) are monotone in p, so the optimum lies on the boundary of the intersection of group-feasible regions, and Algorithm 1 traces this boundary in polynomial time using only calibrated scores and group membership.
The exposition is clear and well-organized, with informative figures (e.g., the feasible-region schematic and the intersection figures) that make the geometric intuition accessible.

Handles limitations honestly: degenerate classifiers are treated in Appendix D, the multi-group feasibility problem is explicitly flagged, and a robustness analysis (|PPV^0-PPV^1| ≤ 2ε, |FOR^0-FOR^1| ≤ 2ε under calibration error ε) is given and corroborated by synthetic and real-data experiments.

Reproducibility is good: public datasets (FICO/TransRisk aggregate statistics, COMPAS, ACS Income), full algorithmic details, and experiment protocols are provided; the ACS experiment is a genuine end-to-end pipeline with held-out evaluation and confidence intervals.
weaknesses: No comparison against existing sufficiency-enforcing post-processing methods (e.g., Baumann et al. 2022, Canetti et al. 2019) or against simple baselines. Experiments only compare to the unconstrained Bayes classifier, so the practical advantage over prior art is only partially demonstrated.

The COMPAS experiment constructs scores that are group-calibrated by assumption (pooled empirical outcome rates per decile), rather than verifying the assumption. This makes it an illustrative sanity check rather than a validation of the method under its core premise.

The central guarantee holds only under exact group-calibration; the worst-case 2ε bound is loose, and the practical sensitivity to calibration quality (bin count, calibration-set size) is explored only through a subsampling study in Appendix J, which shows violations can grow substantially when calibration data is scarce.

The method fundamentally relies on randomized decisions (optimal rules often cannot be realized by a single threshold in one group). The practical downsides of randomization — reproducibility, individual-level fairness, and legal/operational acceptability — are not discussed.

The approach requires the group-wise feasible regions to have a nonempty intersection; for more than two protected groups this can fail, which is acknowledged but leaves the method inapplicable in settings with several groups unless one relaxes exact sufficiency.
